tier_reason: First-party: the README states '18x faster SHA-256 vs Phobos' and links examples/sha256/source/main.d, which times std.digest.sha sha256Of against a SHA-NI path written with inteli intrinsics (1000 x 1,024,000 bytes) and prints both digests; no recorded output, CPU model, LDC version or build type, so it cannot reach A or B.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: LDC; examples/sha256/dub.json sets dflags-ldc ["-mattr=+sha,+sse4.2,+popcnt"] and no build type (dub builds in debug mode unless --build=release is passed); LDC version and the build command used for the 18x figure are not stated.
corrections.caveats: The 18x figure is a README claim without hardware, compiler version, build type or timing output; the benchmark source prints times but the repo does not record results. dub.json sets no buildType, so a plain 'dub run' builds debug; both sides are templates compiled with the same flags, but the ratio depends on the unstated build mode. Baseline is Phobos' portable SHA-256 (std/digest/sha.d uses transformSHA2 for SHA-256; its SSSE3 assembly path covers SHA-1 only), not an optimised library such as OpenSSL, and the fast path relies on dedicated SHA-NI instructions rather than generic SIMD, so the ratio reflects hardware offload as much as the library. On Windows the example's getTickUs defaults to QueryThreadCycleTime scaled by the QPC frequency, which its own comment calls unreliable; both rows use the same timer, so the ratio is unaffected but the printed microseconds may be wrong. Example code is derived from the Crypto++ SHA-SIMD reference (Walton, Blumenthal, Raad) by Johan Engelen (public domain). Claims for dg2d versus Cairo and the 3.5x DConf 2019 talk figure have no numbers on the page and are not part of this entry's tier. Licence file is named COPYING (BSL-1.0, also declared in dub.json). D language, not C++.

notes: Record accurate: README claim, workload (512*2000 bytes of 'a', 1000 iterations), LDC dflags, BSL-1.0, 73 stars and last commit 2026-10-10 all check out. Shortcomings: first-party ratio with no CPU, LDC version or build type; baseline is portable Phobos SHA-256 versus SHA-NI hardware instructions; D library, not C++.

tier_reason: First-party README table (i7-6700, single-threaded, Criterion.rs) gives scalar 888 / sse2 225 / sse41 186 / avx2 108 ms for 2D 4k Fbm and 1,400 / 128 / 94 / 47 ms for 3D 128^3 cell noise, with bench code in benches/benchmarks.rs; rustc version and RUSTFLAGS are not stated and the table predates the current code, so C.

corrections.stars_or_usage: 267 stars, 20 forks; crates.io simdnoise 81,004 total downloads (2,924 recent); latest published version 3.1.6 (2020-05-30), while the repo HEAD (3.1.7 on simdeez 2.0.0-dev3) is unpublished
corrections.caveats: Baseline is the crate's own scalar fallback, not a third-party library (no comparison with FastNoise/FastNoiseSIMD or noise-rs), so the claim shows the benefit of SIMD for this algorithm rather than a win over an independent incumbent. The scalar-to-SSE2 gain on 3D cell noise is 10.9x on 4 lanes (1,400 to 128 ms, derived from page data), which is superlinear and suggests a weak scalar fallback rather than an optimised scalar baseline. The README benchmark table comes from Jack Mott's June 2018 commits ('updated benchmarks'), long before the November 2024 port to simdeez v2, so the numbers do not describe the current code or the published 3.1.6 crate exactly. Compiler version and flags are not stated. In benches/benchmarks.rs the Criterion sample_size and measurement_time settings are applied after the bench_function calls, so they do not take effect. i7-6700 is a 2015 CPU. The repo was transferred from jackmott/rust-simd-noise (that URL now resolves here) and is maintained by Peter Reijnders. There is no LICENSE file in the repo; the licence is declared only in Cargo.toml as 'Apache-2.0/MIT' (same on crates.io). The HN thread was seen only as a search-result title. It is a SIMD noise-generation library built on simdeez rather than an intrinsics wrapper, so the category is a loose fit.

notes: Numbers, CPU and Criterion note all on the README; metadata confirmed (267 stars, last commit 2024-11-20 'port benchmarks to simdeez v2', stale). Shortcomings: self-baseline (own scalar fallback, superlinear 10.9x SSE2 gain on cell noise), 2018 numbers predating the simdeez v2 rewrite, no licence file in repo (Cargo.toml only), loose category fit.

tier_reason: The manual (dated 2026-09-09) only says the inline and SVML-based vector math versions are 'many times faster than standard (scalar) math function libraries' (section 8.3); it has no benchmark, numbers, hardware or flags, and a WebSearch found no independent VCL-vs-libm/SLEEF timing, so D.

corrections.caveats: Tier D: the speed claims have no benchmark, hardware, compiler or flags. Included under the notable-D allowance (1.5k stars, 156 forks, very widely referenced, named repeatedly in HN threads about SIMD wrappers). The manual itself recommends compiler auto-vectorization where it works and positions VCL as the alternative when it fails. The external math-library variant (vectormath_lib.h) needs Intel's proprietary SVML from an Intel compiler installation; only the inline vectormath_*.h functions are fully Apache-2.0. Inline math functions trade subnormal support for speed (per the author's forum remarks, snippet only). x86/x86-64 only; the README says there are no plans to support ARM. Manual date 2026-09-09 matches the latest commit.

notes: Record accurate: no numbers anywhere in the manual or README; Apache-2.0, 1.5k stars, last commit 2026-09-09 (version 2.02.04) confirmed. Shortcomings: no benchmark at all (tier D), SVML variant depends on proprietary Intel library, x86-only.
